Signing and Verifying Tokens

utils/jwt.js wraps jsonwebtoken; env.js's Zod schema grows a new required field to make it possible at all.

// Figure 4.3: two thin wrappers around jsonwebtoken (src/utils/jwt.js)
import jwt from 'jsonwebtoken';
import env from '../config/env.js';

export const signToken = (payload) =>
  jwt.sign(payload, env.JWT_SECRET, { expiresIn: env.JWT_EXPIRES_IN });

export const verifyToken = (token) => jwt.verify(token, env.JWT_SECRET);

signToken is what turns a plain payload — { sub: user.id, role: user.role }, used both places this project issues a token (next two slides) — into the actual header.payload.signature string (previous slide) a client gets back. jwt.sign computes that signature from the payload and env.JWT_SECRET together; change either one, and the signature no longer matches. verifyToken recomputes that same signature from a token it's handed and compares — succeeding (returning the decoded payload) only if nothing about the token has changed since this exact server signed it. expiresIn bounds how long a token stays valid at all — '1d' here — baked into the signature itself, so verifyToken also rejects an otherwise-untampered token that's simply too old.

None of that works without a real secret to sign with, so config/env.js's Zod schema (Lesson 3's config-validation topic) grows a new required field:

// Figure 4.4: JWT_SECRET joins the validated env (src/config/env.js, excerpt)
const envSchema = z.object({
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().positive(),
  DATABASE_URL: z.string().min(1, 'DATABASE_URL is required'),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(16, 'JWT_SECRET must be at least 16 characters'),
  JWT_EXPIRES_IN: z.string().min(1).default('1d'),
});

.min(16, ...) isn't an arbitrary number — a short secret would make jwt.sign's signature guessable, which defeats the entire "tamper-proof" property the previous slide leaned on: anyone who could guess or brute-force JWT_SECRET could forge a token claiming to be any user at all, including an admin. Failing fast here, at startup (the whole point of validating config at all, Lesson 3), catches a weak or missing secret immediately rather than letting the app run with authentication that only looks secure.
